analysis.one_liner: Bans raising prices of essential goods, lodging, and rentals more than 10% after a declared disaster.
analysis.headline: A bill to cap post-disaster price increases at 10% was introduced by one House Democrat and referred to committee, where no action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: After the President declares a major disaster or emergency, the bill would make it illegal to raise prices more than 10% above pre-disaster levels for essential goods and services, hotel rooms, and residential rentals for 30 days (180 days for repair and reconstruction work). It would let the FTC, state attorneys general, and individuals sue violators, with penalties up to $25,000 per violation and money recovered by the FTC directed to disaster-affected communities. The bill has been referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and has received no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: People in disaster areas who need food, water, fuel, generators, medical supplies, hotel rooms, and rentals — or need repairs after the disaster — would be protected from sudden price spikes. Renters in declared disaster areas would get the same 10% cap on rent increases. Individual victims could sue for damages and attorney's fees, and penalties collected by the FTC would go to a fund helping disaster-affected communities [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents and renters in disaster areas

how_it_helps.text: Caps price increases at 10% above pre-disaster levels for essential consumer goods and services, hotel lodging, and residential rentals for 30 days after a presidentially declared disaster, and for 180 days for repair and reconstruction services, when shortages and displacement leave people with the fewest alternatives [S2] [S3].

Adds a second limit: for 30 days, no one may charge more than 50% above their own cost for essential goods, services, or housing if they were not already charging that price before the disaster, targeting sellers whose costs did not rise [S2] [S3].

Gives the FTC enforcement authority, lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents for injunctions, damages, and restitution, and creates a private right of action with triple damages for willful violations plus attorney's fees [S2] [S3].

Directs civil penalties recovered by the FTC into a fund to assist communities in areas affected by the declared disaster, and explicitly preserves stronger state anti-gouging laws rather than preempting them [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Retailers, hotels and motels, landlords, and repair/reconstruction contractors in disaster areas would bear the cost: they could not raise prices more than 10% (or charge more than 50% over cost) during the covered windows, and would face civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation plus private lawsuits and attorney-fee awards for violations [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Retailers, hotels, landlords, contractors in disaster zones

drawbacks.text: A hard 10% cap can be below the actual cost of getting goods into a disaster zone: the bill's own exception only allows higher prices when directly attributable to additional supplier, labor, or material costs plus the seller's customary pre-disaster markup, so genuinely higher logistics costs are covered, but a seller with no established customary markup or with unusual risk could be caught by the cap [S3].

Enforcement relies on identifying a 'pre-disaster price' as of the day before the declaration, which is difficult in fast-moving emergencies and could invite litigation over what the baseline was; the private right of action carries mandatory attorney's fees, which could generate suits after every declaration [S3].

The bill sets a maximum total civil penalty of $25,000 per person for all violations from the same or related acts — even though each violation can be counted separately up to $25,000 — a cap that is small relative to the revenue a large chain could gain from gouging across a region [S3].

Opponents of disaster price-gouging laws generally argue that letting prices rise encourages suppliers to rush goods into affected areas and prevents shortages; this bill's cost-based exception is designed to allow that, but the 10% ceiling still limits how strongly the price signal can work [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers in disaster zones is direct and large: people evacuating or recovering after a disaster have no realistic alternative sellers, so price spikes there are pure transfers, and the bill targets exactly those moments while allowing cost-based increases, seasonal hotel adjustments, and agreed rent increases [S3]. The main costs fall on sellers who genuinely face higher emergency logistics costs not fully captured by the exception, and the $25,000 total-penalty cap makes federal enforcement fairly weak — but state AG and private suits fill some of that gap. On balance, the consumer protection outweighs the cost, though the bill is modest in scope and untested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it; with Congress still in session it could still move, though bills that sit this long in committee rarely do.

narrative.text: Rep. Laura Friedman introduced the Stop Disaster Price Gouging Act on March 27, 2025, joined by one cosponsor, Rep. Brad Sherman [S3] [S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].

If enacted, it would prohibit price increases over 10% above pre-disaster levels for essential goods and services, hotel lodging, and rentals for 30 days after a presidential disaster declaration (180 days for repair and reconstruction services), with FTC, state, and private enforcement [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, no one has won or lost: the bill simply sits in committee. Sellers of essential goods, hotels, landlords, and contractors are better off than they would be under an enacted ban, since nothing currently restricts their pricing in federally declared disaster areas beyond existing state laws.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No outcome yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Laura Friedman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a federal disaster price-gouging ban

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its referral on March 27, 2025; the record shows no action beyond referral [S5]

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are Democrats and the bill has drawn no Republican cosponsors, but there has been no vote or recorded opposition to show how the parties line up.

industries.note: Disaster-driven lodging surges are a well-known source of gouging complaints; the bill would cap rates at 10% above pre-disaster levels for 30 days, exempting only regularly scheduled seasonal adjustments. It also bars charging more than 50% above cost if that price was not charged before the disaster.

After a disaster declaration, rents in affected areas could rise no more than 10% for 30 days, except where increases reflect documented repair costs or were contractually agreed before the disaster. This directly limits rent spikes on displaced residents.

Contractors would face the 10% cap for a much longer window — 180 days — covering the period when homeowners most need roof, plumbing, and structural repairs. Cost-based increases up to the customary markup are excepted.

industries.industry: Retailers and fuel sellers of essential goods (grocers, hardware, gasoline)
industries.note: Stores selling food, water, generators, medical supplies, and motor fuel could not raise prices more than 10% for 30 days after a declaration, and could not exceed 50% above their own cost if that was not their prior price. The exception for higher supplier costs and tariffs limits the hit when their own costs genuinely rise.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one cosponsor, no Republican support, and no committee action since referral in March 2025. Most bills referred to a committee with no scheduled hearing die there quietly when the Congress ends in January 2027; a realistic path forward would require the committee to hold a hearing and mark it up, which there is no sign of.
